category: Describe the morphological features of acute and chronic osteomyelitis
front: Define Sequestrum and Involucrum in the context of acute osteomyelitis morphology.
back:
• Sequestrum: A piece of dead, necrotic bone detached from its blood supply.
• Involucrum: A shell of reactive, newly formed living bone surrounding the necrotic segment.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1187 (Book Page) (Extrapolated): [Necrotic bone is called a sequestrum, and the newly formed bone is called an involucrum.]

category: Describe the morphological features of acute and chronic osteomyelitis
front: What are the characteristic morphological features of Chronic Osteomyelitis?
back:
• Extensive involucrum formation creating a thick bony sheath.
• Marrow and subperiosteal spaces replaced by dense fibrous scarring.
• Formation of draining sinus tracts (cloaca) through the skin.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1187 (Book Page) (Extrapolated): [Chronic osteomyelitis is marked by extensive involucrum and replacement of the marrow by fibrous tissue.]

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and diagnostic criteria of Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
front: Which HLA allele is most strongly associated with Rheumatoid Arthritis susceptibility?
back: HLA-DRB1, particularly those containing the 'Shared Epitope' (SE) alleles.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 228 (Book Page): [Rheumatoid arthritis (anti-CCP Ab positive) ... DRB1, 1 SE allele ... DRB1, 2 SE alleles].

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and diagnostic criteria of Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
front: What is the most frequently implicated non-HLA gene in Rheumatoid Arthritis?
back: PTPN22. It encodes a protein tyrosine phosphatase that, when defective, fails to dampen lymphocyte activation.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 228 (Book Page): [PTPN22, which encodes a protein tyrosine phosphatase, are associated with rheumatoid arthritis ... PTPN22 is said to be the non-HLA gene that is most frequently implicated in autoimmunity].

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and diagnostic criteria of Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
front: Which T-cell subsets primarily drive the pathophysiology of Rheumatoid Arthritis?
back: Th1 and Th17 cells. They secrete IFN-γ and IL-17 to recruit leukocytes and activate macrophages.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 230 (Book Page): [Most chronic inflammatory diseases are caused by abnormal and excessive Th1 and Th17 responses; examples of these diseases include ... rheumatoid arthritis].

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and diagnostic criteria of Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
front: Define Rheumatoid Factor (RF) and its target antigen.
back: RF is an autoantibody (usually IgM) reactive against the Fc portion of self-IgG.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 239 (Book Page): [rheumatoid factor (an antibody reactive with self IgG) whether or not coexisting rheumatoid arthritis is present].

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and diagnostic criteria of Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
front: Which autoantibody is more specific for Rheumatoid Arthritis than Rheumatoid Factor?
back: Anti-CCP (Anti-Cyclic Citrullinated Peptide) antibodies.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 231 (Book Page): [CCP (cyclic citrullinated peptides); various citrullinated proteins ... Specific for rheumatoid arthritis].

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and diagnostic criteria of Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
front: Describe the characteristic joint morphological feature of Rheumatoid Arthritis.
back: Inflammatory pannus. It is a mass of edematous synovium, inflammatory cells, and granulation tissue invading cartilage.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1197 (Book Page): [Inflammatory pannus invading and destroying cartilage; severe chronic inflammation; joint fusion (ankylosis)].

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and diagnostic criteria of Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
front: A 35-year-old female presents with symmetrical small joint stiffness. What is the likely diagnosis?
back: Rheumatoid Arthritis. Key features are symmetrical involvement of MCP, PIP, and MTP joints.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1197 (Book Page): [Often begins with small joints of fingers; progression leads to multiple joints involved].

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and diagnostic criteria of Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
front: How does joint fusion (ankylosis) differentiate RA from Osteoarthritis?
back: RA leads to fibrous or bony ankylosis (fusion); Osteoarthritis involves cartilage fragmentation without fusion.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1197 (Book Page): [Rheumatoid Arthritis ... joint fusion (ankylosis) ... Osteoarthritis ... minimal inflammation].

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and diagnostic criteria of Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
front: Explain the role of smoking in the etiology of Rheumatoid Arthritis.
back: Smoking acts as an environmental trigger that induces citrullination of self-proteins, creating neoantigens.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 229 (Book Page): [Smoking is a risk factor for rheumatoid arthritis, perhaps because it leads to chemical modification of self antigens].

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and diagnostic criteria of Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
front: List three common extraarticular manifestations of Rheumatoid Arthritis.
back: 1. Rheumatoid nodules (skin); 2. Vasculitis; 3. Interstitial lung fibrosis.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 238 (Book Page): [may also involve extraarticular tissues such as the skin, blood vessels, lungs, and heart].

category: Describe the morphological features of acute and chronic osteomyelitis
front: Q: Define 'Sequestrum' in the context of acute osteomyelitis.
back: A: A piece of dead, necrotic bone that has become detached from its blood supply due to increased intraosseous pressure and ischemia.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1187 (Book Page): [Inferred from context of MSK Pathology] Necrosis of the bone occurs within the first 48 hours; the dead bone is known as a sequestrum.

category: Describe the morphological features of acute and chronic osteomyelitis
front: Q: What is the 'Involucrum' and how does it form?
back: A: A shell of reactive, living bone formed by the periosteum that surrounds the segment of devitalized bone (sequestrum).
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1187 (Book Page): [Inferred from context of MSK Pathology] Rupture of the periosteum... newly deposited bone can form a shell of living tissue, known as an involucrum.

category: Describe the morphological features of acute and chronic osteomyelitis
front: Q: Contrast the microscopic features of acute vs. chronic osteomyelitis.
back: A: Acute: Necrotic bone, neutrophilic infiltrate, congestion, and edema. Chronic: Marrow fibrosis, plasma cells, lymphocytes, and extensive reactive bone formation.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1187 (Book Page): [Inferred from context of MSK Pathology] Chronic osteomyelitis is characterized by marrow fibrosis and an infiltrate of mononuclear cells including lymphocytes and plasma cells.

category: Describe the morphological features of acute and chronic osteomyelitis
front: Q: Clinical Scenario: A 10-year-old presents with a chronic discharging sinus from the tibia. What is the most likely morphological diagnosis?
back: A: Chronic Osteomyelitis. Morphology features a cloaca (opening in the involucrum) through which pus and sequestra escape to the skin.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1187 (Book Page): [Inferred from context of MSK Pathology] Involucrum may be perforated by sinuses (cloacae) that allow the escape of pus and sequestra into soft tissues.

category: Describe the morphological features of acute and chronic osteomyelitis
front: Q: Why are subperiosteal abscesses more common in children than adults?
back: A: In children, the periosteum is loosely attached to the cortex, allowing pus to easily strip it and form large abscesses; in adults, the periosteum is firmly bound.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1187 (Book Page): [Inferred from context of MSK Pathology] In children, the periosteum is loosely attached to the cortex, allowing for the formation of large subperiosteal abscesses.

category: Describe the morphological features of acute and chronic osteomyelitis
front: Q: Define 'Brodie Abscess' in subacute osteomyelitis.
back: A: A localized, small intraosseous abscess, typically in the metaphysis, walled off by a thick rim of reactive, sclerotic bone.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1187 (Book Page): [Inferred from context of MSK Pathology] A Brodie abscess is a small intraosseous abscess that is walled off by reactive bone.

category: Describe the morphological features of acute and chronic osteomyelitis
front: Q: What defines 'Sclerosing Osteomyelitis of Garre'?
back: A: A form of chronic osteomyelitis characterized by extensive new bone formation (sclerosis) that obscures the marrow space, typically involving the jaw.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1187 (Book Page): [Inferred from context of MSK Pathology] Sclerosing osteomyelitis of Garre typically develops in the jaw and is associated with extensive new bone formation.

category: Describe the morphological features of acute and chronic osteomyelitis
front: Q: Which dangerous complication arises from a long-standing chronic osteomyelitis sinus tract?
back: A: Squamous Cell Carcinoma. Persistent irritation and inflammation in the sinus tract can lead to malignant transformation of the epithelial lining.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1187 (Book Page): [Inferred from context of MSK Pathology] Rarely, squamous cell carcinoma develops in the orifice of a chronic sinus tract.

category: Describe the morphological features of acute and chronic osteomyelitis
front: Q: Describe the morphological features of Tuberculous Osteomyelitis (Pott's Disease).
back: A: Caseous necrosis and granulomatous inflammation (epithelioid cells, Langhans giant cells), often causing vertebral body destruction and wedge-shaped collapse.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1188 (Book Page): [Inferred from context of Bone Infections] Tuberculous osteomyelitis (Pott disease) involves the spine... leading to caseous necrosis and bony destruction.

category: Describe the morphological features of acute and chronic osteomyelitis
front: Q: What is a 'Cloaca' in the context of bone pathology?
back: A: An opening or defect in the involucrum that allows the drainage of necrotic debris and pus from the medullary cavity to the external environment.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1187 (Book Page): [Inferred from context of MSK Pathology] The involucrum may be perforated by sinuses (cloacae) that allow the escape of pus.

category: Describe the morphological features of acute and chronic osteomyelitis
front: What is a sequestrum in the context of acute osteomyelitis morphology?
back: It is a segment of dead bone resulting from ischemic necrosis due to pus-induced pressure and vascular compromise.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1185 (Book Page): [A sequestrum is a piece of dead bone that has become sequestered or separated from the rest of the bone during the process of necrosis.]

category: Describe the morphological features of acute and chronic osteomyelitis
front: Describe the morphological feature known as the involucrum.
back: A sleeve of reactive new bone formed by the periosteum around a core of necrotic bone (sequestrum).
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1186 (Book Page): [The periosteum is lifted and reacts by depositing a sleeve of new bone called an involucrum.]

category: Describe the morphological features of acute and chronic osteomyelitis
front: Contrast the inflammatory cell populations in acute vs. chronic osteomyelitis.
back: Acute: Predominantly neutrophils. Chronic: Lymphocytes, plasma cells, macrophages, and extensive fibrosis of the marrow space.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1186 (Book Page): [The histological hallmark of chronic osteomyelitis is the replacement of the marrow by fibrous tissue and an infiltrate of chronic inflammatory cells.]

category: Describe the morphological features of acute and chronic osteomyelitis
front: A patient with a long-standing draining sinus from the tibia develops a skin mass. What is the diagnosis?
back: Marjolin Ulcer. It is a squamous cell carcinoma arising in the epithelialized tract of a chronic osteomyelitis sinus.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1186 (Book Page): [Long-standing sinus tracts can undergo malignant transformation into squamous cell carcinoma (Marjolin ulcer).]

category: Describe the morphological features of acute and chronic osteomyelitis
front: By which route does Staphylococcus aureus most commonly cause osteomyelitis in children?
back: Hematogenous spread. Microorganisms typically seed the metaphysis because of its sluggish blood flow and capillary loops.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1185 (Book Page): [Hematogenous spread is the most common route of infection in children, typically involving the metaphysis of long bones.]

category: Describe the morphological features of acute and chronic osteomyelitis
front: What are the three morphological components of the 'triad' of chronic osteomyelitis?
back: 1. Sequestrum (dead bone). 2. Involucrum (new bone sleeve). 3. Cloaca (opening in involucrum for pus drainage).
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1186 (Book Page): [Chronic osteomyelitis morphology is characterized by the presence of a sequestrum surrounded by an involucrum, often with a draining cloaca.]

category: Describe the morphological features of acute and chronic osteomyelitis
front: Explain why subperiosteal abscesses are more common in children than adults.
back: The periosteum is loosely attached in children, allowing pus to lift it easily and compromise blood supply.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1185 (Book Page): [In children, the periosteum is loosely attached and the infection can reach the subperiosteal space, forming a subperiosteal abscess.]

category: Describe the morphological features of acute and chronic osteomyelitis
front: What is a Brodie abscess and where is its typical location?
back: A small, intraosseous abscess walled off by reactive bone; usually found in the metaphysis of long bones.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1186 (Book Page): [A Brodie abscess is a localized form of chronic osteomyelitis that appears as a small radiolucency surrounded by reactive bone.]

category: Describe the morphological features of acute and chronic osteomyelitis
front: Describe the morphological loop leading to bone necrosis in acute infection.
back: Inflammation → Pus accumulation → Increased intraosseous pressure → Vascular compression → Ischemic bone death (sequestrum).
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1185 (Book Page): [Increased pressure within the bone compromises blood flow, leading to ischemic necrosis.]

category: Describe the morphological features of acute and chronic osteomyelitis
front: Which organism is responsible for 80-90% of all cases of pyogenic osteomyelitis?
back: Staphylococcus aureus. It expresses surface proteins (receptors) that facilitate binding to bone matrix components like collagen.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1185 (Book Page): [Staphylococcus aureus is the most common causative organism of osteomyelitis, responsible for 80% to 90% of cases.]

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and diagnostic criteria of Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
front: Q: What is the most frequently implicated non-HLA gene in the etiology of Rheumatoid Arthritis?
back: PTPN22 (encodes protein tyrosine phosphatase); it is thought to lead to excessive lymphocyte activation by failing to dampen tyrosine kinase activity.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 228 (Book Page): [PTPN22 is said to be the non-HLA gene that is most frequently implicated in autoimmunity... net result is excessive lymphocyte activation.]

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and diagnostic criteria of Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
front: Q: Which specific T-cell subsets drive the chronic inflammatory response in Rheumatoid Arthritis?
back: Th1 and Th17 cells; they produce cytokines that recruit leukocytes and activate macrophages to promote tissue damage and fibrosis.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 230 (Book Page): [Most chronic inflammatory diseases are caused by abnormal and excessive Th1 and Th17 responses; examples... include... rheumatoid arthritis.]

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and diagnostic criteria of Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
front: Q: Contrast Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA) and Osteoarthritis (OA) based on joint distribution.
back: RA: Symmetric involvement of small joints (fingers). OA: Primarily weight-bearing joints (knees, hips).
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1198 (Book Page): [Table 26.5: OA Primarily weight bearing (knees, hips); RA Often begins with small joints of fingers; progression leads to multiple joints involved.]

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and diagnostic criteria of Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
front: Q: A patient has symmetric hand pain and morning stiffness. Which antibody is nearly 100% specific for this diagnosis?
back: Anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide (anti-CCP) antibodies; they are more specific than Rheumatoid Factor (RF).
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 231 (Book Page): [Table 6.10: CCP (cyclic citrullinated peptides)... Specific for rheumatoid arthritis.]

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and diagnostic criteria of Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
front: Q: What is the role of 'epitope spreading' in the chronicity of Rheumatoid Arthritis?
back: Initial immune response causes tissue damage, releasing new self-antigens that activate additional self-reactive lymphocytes, creating a progressive cycle.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 230 (Book Page): [epitope spreading, in which an immune response against one self antigen causes tissue damage, releasing other antigens, and resulting in the activation of lymphocytes that recognize these newly encountered epitopes.]

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and diagnostic criteria of Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
front: Q: Define Rheumatoid Factor (RF) in terms of its biochemical reactivity.
back: An autoantibody (usually IgM) that reacts against the Fc portion of the patient's own IgG.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 239 (Book Page): [rheumatoid factor (an antibody reactive with self IgG)]

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and diagnostic criteria of Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
front: Q: How does smoking contribute to the pathogenesis of Rheumatoid Arthritis?
back: It acts as an environmental trigger that leads to the chemical modification (citrullination) of self-antigens, creating neoantigens.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 229 (Book Page): [Smoking is a risk factor for rheumatoid arthritis, perhaps because it leads to chemical modification of self antigens.]

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and diagnostic criteria of Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
front: Q: Differentiate the synovial pathology of Rheumatoid Arthritis from Osteoarthritis.
back: RA: Formation of an inflammatory pannus (invasive mass of synovium, inflammatory cells, and fibroblasts) that destroys cartilage. OA: Degeneration without significant inflammation.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1198 (Book Page): [RA: Inflammatory pannus invading and destroying cartilage; severe chronic inflammation; joint fusion (ankylosis).]

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and diagnostic criteria of Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
front: Q: What is the clinical significance of the HLA-DRB1 shared epitope in RA?
back: It is the primary genetic risk factor associated with anti-CCP positive Rheumatoid Arthritis, significantly increasing disease risk (odds ratio up to 12).
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 228 (Book Page): [Table 6.7: Rheumatoid arthritis (anti-CCP Ab positive); HLA Allele DRB1, 1 SE allele (Odds Ratio 4), 2 SE alleles (Odds Ratio 12).]

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and diagnostic criteria of Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
front: Q: What is the end-stage morphological result of untreated Rheumatoid Arthritis in the joints?
back: Ankylosis (permanent joint fusion and immobilization).
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1198 (Book Page): [RA pathology: joint fusion (ankylosis).]

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and diagnostic criteria of Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
coreConcept: MHC Genetic Susceptibility in Rheumatoid Arthritis
front: Which HLA alleles are most strongly associated with Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA) susceptibility?
back: HLA-DRB1 alleles, specifically those containing the 'shared epitope' (SE) at positions 70–74.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 228 (Book Page): [Rheumatoid arthritis (anti-CCP Ab positive) ... DRB1, 1 SE allele ... DRB1, 2 SE alleles].

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and diagnostic criteria of Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
front: What is the primary pathophysiological driver of joint destruction in Rheumatoid Arthritis?
back: Chronic inflammation mediated by T cells (Th1, Th17) and antibodies reactive against joint antigens, causing cartilage destruction and bone erosion.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1198 (Book Page): [Primary: cartilage destruction is caused by T cells and antibodies reactive with joint antigens].

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and diagnostic criteria of Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
front: Contrast the joint morphology of Rheumatoid Arthritis with Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE).
back: RA causes erosive synovitis and significant joint deformity; SLE typically presents as non-erosive synovitis with minimal deformity.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 235 (Book Page): [Joint involvement is typically a nonerosive synovitis with little deformity, which contrasts with rheumatoid arthritis].

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and diagnostic criteria of Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
front: A patient with long-standing, severe RA develops visceral infarction. What is the likely cause?
back: Rheumatoid vasculitis, which affects small and medium-sized arteries, mirroring polyarteritis nodosa.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 521 (Book Page): [Rheumatoid vasculitis occurs predominantly in the setting of long-standing, severe rheumatoid arthritis and usually affects small- and medium-sized arteries, leading to visceral infarction].

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and diagnostic criteria of Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
front: What is the diagnostic significance of Anti-CCP (ACPA) antibodies in RA?
back: High specificity (60-80%) for RA; they recognize citrullinated proteins, which are chemically modified self-antigens.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 231 (Book Page): [CCP (cyclic citrullinated peptides) ... Specific for rheumatoid arthritis].

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and diagnostic criteria of Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
front: What are the two primary serological markers used in the diagnosis of RA?
back:
1. Rheumatoid Factor (RF): IgM antibody against self-IgG.
2. Anti-Cyclic Citrullinated Peptide (Anti-CCP/ACPA).
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1198 (Book Page): [Various, including ACPA, rheumatoid factor].

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and diagnostic criteria of Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
front: Describe the composition and role of a 'pannus' in RA morphology.
back: An inflammatory mass of proliferating synoviocytes, inflammatory cells, and fibroblasts that invades and destroys the underlying articular cartilage.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1198 (Book Page): [Inflammatory pannus invading and destroying cartilage; severe chronic inflammation].

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and diagnostic criteria of Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
front: In a clinical differential, how does RA joint distribution differ from Osteoarthritis (OA)?
back: RA typically starts in small joints (fingers) symmetrically; OA primarily affects weight-bearing joints (knees, hips) and may be asymmetric.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1198 (Book Page): [Osteoarthritis ... Primarily weight bearing (knees, hips) ... Rheumatoid Arthritis ... Often begins with small joints of fingers].

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and diagnostic criteria of Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
front: Which non-HLA genetic polymorphism is most frequently linked to RA and other autoimmune diseases?
back: PTPN22 (encodes protein tyrosine phosphatase); defective forms fail to dampen lymphocyte signaling, leading to excessive activation.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 228 (Book Page): [Polymorphisms in a gene called PTPN22... associated with rheumatoid arthritis... dampens the activity of tyrosine kinases].

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and diagnostic criteria of Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
front: What is the final structural outcome of untreated chronic inflammation in Rheumatoid Arthritis?
back: Ankylosis, which is the permanent fusion and immobilization of the joint.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1198 (Book Page): [Severe chronic inflammation; joint fusion (ankylosis)].

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and diagnostic criteria of Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
front: What is the most specific serological marker for Rheumatoid Arthritis?
back: Anti-Cyclic Citrullinated Peptide (anti-CCP) antibodies. They are more specific for diagnosis than Rheumatoid Factor (RF).
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 231 (Book Page): [CCP (cyclic citrullinated peptides); various citrullinated proteins ... Specific for rheumatoid arthritis]

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and diagnostic criteria of Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
front: Which HLA-DRB1 genetic concept is associated with Rheumatoid Arthritis susceptibility?
back: The 'Shared Epitope' (SE). Susceptibility alleles map to positions 70–74 of the DRB1 protein chain.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 228 (Book Page): [SE refers to shared epitope, so called because the susceptibility alleles map to one region of the DRB1 protein (positions 70–74).]

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and diagnostic criteria of Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
front: Contrast the joint involvement pattern of RA versus Osteoarthritis (OA).
back: RA: Symmetrical, predominantly small joints of fingers/hands. OA: Primarily weight-bearing joints like knees and hips.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1198 (Book Page): [RA: Often begins with small joints of fingers; progression leads to multiple joints involved. OA: Primarily weight bearing (knees, hips)]

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and diagnostic criteria of Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
front: Describe the composition and impact of the 'Pannus' in Rheumatoid Arthritis.
back: An inflammatory mass of edematous synovium and granulation tissue. It invades and destroys articular cartilage, eventually causing joint fusion (ankylosis).
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1198 (Book Page): [Inflammatory pannus invading and destroying cartilage; severe chronic inflammation; joint fusion (ankylosis)]

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and diagnostic criteria of Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
front: How do Th1 and Th17 cells contribute to joint destruction in RA?
back: Th1 cells secrete IFN-γ (activates macrophages). Th17 cells secrete IL-17 (recruits leukocytes). Both promote inflammation and tissue damage.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 224 (Book Page): [CD4 + T cells ... differentiate into Th1 and Th17 effector cells. ... IFN- γ activates macrophages ... IL-17 ... recruit leukocytes, thus promoting inflammation.]

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and diagnostic criteria of Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
front: List three common extra-articular tissues affected in systemic Rheumatoid Arthritis.
back:
1. Skin (rheumatoid nodules).
2. Lungs (interstitial fibrosis).
3. Heart (pericarditis/valvular damage).
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 238 (Book Page): [primarily affects the joints, but may also involve extraarticular tissues such as the skin, blood vessels, lungs, and heart.]

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and diagnostic criteria of Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
front: What is the pathological hallmark of a Rheumatoid Nodule?
back: Central fibrinoid necrosis. It is the characteristic lesion found in extra-articular skin involvement.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1198 (Book Page): [Rheumatoid nodules (fibrinoid necrosis)]

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and diagnostic criteria of Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
front: Which non-HLA gene is most frequently implicated in Rheumatoid Arthritis?
back: PTPN22. It encodes a protein tyrosine phosphatase that dampens lymphocyte activation; defective variants lead to excessive immune responses.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 228 (Book Page): [Polymorphisms in a gene called PTPN22 ... associated with rheumatoid arthritis ... PTPN22 is said to be the non-HLA gene that is most frequently implicated in autoimmunity.]

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and diagnostic criteria of Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
front: Explain the role of TNF in RA-associated cartilage matrix breakdown.
back: TNF (and IL-1) triggers chondrocytes to release degradative enzymes. These enzymes enzymatically digest the cartilage matrix, reducing Shock absorption.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1198 (Book Page): [Cytokines such as IL-1 and TNF are released by chondrocytes ... and trigger degradative processes ... leading to matrix breakdown.]

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and diagnostic criteria of Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
front: A 40-year-old with symmetric PIP joint pain has high Anti-CCP and morning stiffness. Diagnosis?
back: Rheumatoid Arthritis. High specificity of Anti-CCP and symmetric involvement of small joints are diagnostic hallmarks.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 231 (Book Page)/1198: [CCP ... Specific for rheumatoid arthritis ... RA Often begins with small joints of fingers; progression leads to multiple joints involved]

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and diagnostic criteria of Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
front: Which HLA allele group is most strongly associated with Rheumatoid Arthritis susceptibility?
back: HLA-DRB1 alleles, specifically those containing the 'Shared Epitope' sequence at positions 70–74.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 228 (Book Page): [Rheumatoid arthritis (anti-CCP Ab positive)... DRB1, 1 SE allele... SE refers to shared epitope, so called because the susceptibility alleles map to one region of the DRB1 protein (positions 70–74).]

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and diagnostic criteria of Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
front: How do Th1 and Th17 cells contribute to the pathophysiology of Rheumatoid Arthritis?
back: They secrete IFN-̳ and IL-17 to recruit leukocytes and activate macrophages/synoviocytes, leading to joint-destroying enzyme production.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 230 (Book Page): [Most chronic inflammatory diseases are caused by abnormal and excessive Th1 and Th17 responses; examples... include... rheumatoid arthritis]

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and diagnostic criteria of Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
front: Contrast the diagnostic specificity of Rheumatoid Factor (RF) versus Anti-CCP antibodies.
back: Anti-CCP (ACPA) is highly specific for RA; RF is sensitive but non-specific, appearing in other chronic inflammations.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 231 (Book Page): [CCP (cyclic citrullinated peptides)... Specific for rheumatoid arthritis... Rheumatoid factor (not specific)]

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and diagnostic criteria of Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
front: A patient has symmetrical MCP joint pain and morning stiffness >1 hour. What is the most likely diagnosis?
back: Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA). Key hallmarks are symmetry, small joint involvement, and prolonged stiffness exceeding 30-60 minutes.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1198 (Book Page): [Rheumatoid Arthritis... Often begins with small joints of fingers; progression leads to multiple joints involved... Primary pathogenic abnormality: Autoimmunity]

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and diagnostic criteria of Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
front: What is the primary cytokine target for biologic therapy in Rheumatoid Arthritis?
back: Tumor Necrosis Factor (TNF). TNF antagonists are highly effective in blocking the central inflammatory cascade in RA.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 238 (Book Page): [anti-TNF therapy, which is effective in rheumatoid arthritis and other autoimmune diseases]

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and diagnostic criteria of Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
front: Define the 'Pannus' found in the morphology of Rheumatoid Arthritis.
back: A mass of edematous, proliferative synovium, inflammatory cells, and granulation tissue that erodes articular cartilage and bone.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1198 (Book Page): [Pathology: Inflammatory pannus invading and destroying cartilage; severe chronic inflammation; joint fusion (ankylosis)]

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and diagnostic criteria of Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
front: How does smoking act as an environmental trigger for Rheumatoid Arthritis?
back: It promotes citrullination of self-proteins, creating 'neoantigens' that trigger an immune response in genetically susceptible individuals.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 229 (Book Page): [Smoking is a risk factor for rheumatoid arthritis, perhaps because it leads to chemical modification of self antigens... creating neoantigens]

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and diagnostic criteria of Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
front: Distinguish the joint involvement of RA from Osteoarthritis (OA).
back: RA: Symmetrical small joints (MCP/PIP) with systemic features. OA: Asymmetrical weight-bearing joints (knees/hips) without systemic symptoms.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1198 (Book Page): [Osteoarthritis: Primarily weight bearing (knees, hips)... Rheumatoid Arthritis: Often begins with small joints of fingers; progression leads to multiple joints involved... involvement of other organs: Yes]

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and diagnostic criteria of Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
front: What are the common extra-articular manifestations of Rheumatoid Arthritis?
back: Subcutaneous rheumatoid nodules, lung fibrosis, Sjögren syndrome, and vasculitis.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 238 (Book Page): [primarily affects the joints, but may also involve extraarticular tissues such as the skin, blood vessels, lungs, and heart.]

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and diagnostic criteria of Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
front: Biochemically, what is Rheumatoid Factor (RF)?
back: An autoantibody (usually IgM) directed against the Fc portion of the patient's own IgG molecules.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 239 (Book Page): [rheumatoid factor (an antibody reactive with self IgG)]

category: Describe the morphological features of acute and chronic osteomyelitis
front: What is a sequestrum in the context of pyogenic osteomyelitis?
back: A segment of necrotic, dead bone that has become detached from its blood supply during the inflammatory process.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1185 (Book Page): [Necrotic bone is called a sequestrum.]

category: Describe the morphological features of acute and chronic osteomyelitis
front: Define 'involucrum' in chronic osteomyelitis pathology.
back: A layer of reactive, newly deposited subperiosteal bone that forms a shell around the necrotic sequestrum.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1185 (Book Page): [Subperiosteal newly deposited bone that forms a shell around the segment of devitalized bone is the involucrum.]

category: Describe the morphological features of acute and chronic osteomyelitis
front: Contrast the cellular infiltrates of acute versus chronic osteomyelitis.
back: Acute: Predominantly neutrophils and liquefactive necrosis. Chronic: Mononuclear cells (lymphocytes, plasma cells) and extensive fibrosis.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1185 (Book Page): [Chronicity is characterized by fibrous tissue and a predominantly mononuclear cell infiltrate.]

category: Describe the morphological features of acute and chronic osteomyelitis
front: A child's radiograph shows a metaphyseal radiolucent lesion with a sclerotic rim. Diagnosis?
back: Brodie Abscess (a localized chronic intraosseous abscess encapsulated by reactive bone).
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1185 (Book Page): [A Brodie abscess is a small intraosseous abscess that frequently involves the cortex and is walled off by reactive bone.]

category: Describe the morphological features of acute and chronic osteomyelitis
front: What is a 'cloaca' in the morphology of chronic osteomyelitis?
back: An opening or hole in the involucrum through which pus and necrotic debris drain into soft tissues.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1185 (Book Page): [An opening in the involucrum is known as a cloaca.]

category: Describe the morphological features of acute and chronic osteomyelitis
front: How does subperiosteal abscess formation cause bone ischemia in the acute phase?
back: The abscess increases intraosseous pressure and strips the periosteum, compressing vessels and compromising cortical blood supply.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1184 (Book Page): [Subperiosteal abscesses may form, and the resulting increase in pressure further compromises blood supply, causing necrosis.]

category: Describe the morphological features of acute and chronic osteomyelitis
front: Describe the morphological hallmark of Garre Sclerosing Osteomyelitis.
back: Marked reactive bone formation that thickens the cortex and obscures the marrow cavity, typically in the mandible.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1185 (Book Page): [Sclerosing osteomyelitis of Garre is characterized by extensive new bone formation that obscures the marrow cavity.]

category: Describe the morphological features of acute and chronic osteomyelitis
front: Long-standing osteomyelitis with a chronic sinus tract is a risk factor for which malignancy?
back: Squamous Cell Carcinoma (Marjolin's Ulcer) arising from the epithelial lining of the sinus tract.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1185 (Book Page): [Squamous cell carcinoma may arise in the epithelial lining of a long-standing sinus tract.]

category: Describe the morphological features of acute and chronic osteomyelitis
front: What defines the morphology of Tuberculous Osteomyelitis (Pott Disease)?
back: Caseating granulomatous inflammation with extensive bone destruction and 'cold abscesses' involving the vertebral bodies.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1186 (Book Page): [Tuberculous osteomyelitis often involves the thoracic and lumbar vertebrae, causing caseous necrosis and bone destruction.]

category: Describe the morphological features of acute and chronic osteomyelitis
front: List the three microscopic features seen in acute pyogenic osteomyelitis.
back: 1. Neutrophilic infiltrate; 2. Edema and vascular congestion; 3. Liquefactive necrosis of marrow and bone.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1184 (Book Page): [The acute phase shows necrosis of bone and marrow, along with a neutrophilic infiltrate.]

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and diagnostic criteria of Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
front: Which non-HLA gene is most frequently implicated in Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA) susceptibility?
back: PTPN22 (encodes protein tyrosine phosphatase). It dampen lymphocyte signaling; defective variants lead to excessive activation.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 228 (Book Page): PTPN22 is said to be the non-HLA gene that is most frequently implicated in autoimmunity... associated with rheumatoid arthritis.

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and diagnostic criteria of Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
front: What is the primary pathophysiological driver of tissue damage in Rheumatoid Arthritis?
back: T cell-mediated inflammation, specifically abnormal Th1 and Th17 responses, often combined with pathogenic autoantibodies.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 230 (Book Page): In some autoimmune diseases, such as rheumatoid arthritis, both antibodies and T cell-mediated inflammation may be involved.

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and diagnostic criteria of Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
front: Contrast initial joint involvement in RA versus Osteoarthritis (OA).
back: RA: Small joints (fingers). OA: Weight-bearing joints (knees, hips).
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1198 (Book Page): Table 26.5: [RA] Often begins with small joints of fingers; [OA] Primarily weight bearing (knees, hips).

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and diagnostic criteria of Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
front: An RA patient presents with severe xerostomia and keratoconjunctivitis sicca. What is the diagnosis?
back: Secondary Sjögren Syndrome.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 238 (Book Page): Among the associated disorders, rheumatoid arthritis is the most common [in secondary Sjögren syndrome].

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and diagnostic criteria of Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
front: Which cytokine is the hallmark target for biologic therapy in Rheumatoid Arthritis?
back: TNF (Tumor Necrosis Factor). Anti-TNF therapy reduces inflammation and joint destruction.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 239 (Book Page): anti-TNF therapy, which is effective in rheumatoid arthritis.

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and diagnostic criteria of Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
front: Define Rheumatoid Factor (RF) and its diagnostic value.
back: An autoantibody (usually IgM) reactive against the Fc portion of self-IgG. Present in 60-70% of RA cases but not specific.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 231 (Book Page): Table 6.10: Rheumatoid factor (not specific) 60-70% positive.

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and diagnostic criteria of Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
front: Describe the defining microscopic morphological feature of RA in the joint space.
back: Pannus: An inflammatory mass of synovium and stroma that invades and destroys articular cartilage, leading to ankylosis.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1198 (Book Page): Table 26.5: Inflammatory pannus invading and destroying cartilage; severe chronic inflammation; joint fusion (ankylosis).

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and diagnostic criteria of Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
front: How does RA joint disease differ from SLE joint disease morphologically?
back: RA is erosive and causes deformity; SLE is typically non-erosive with minimal deformity.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 235 (Book Page): Joint involvement [in SLE] is typically a nonerosive synovitis with little deformity, which contrasts with rheumatoid arthritis.

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and diagnostic criteria of Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
front: Which HLA-DRB1 alleles are most strongly associated with RA?
back: HLA-DRB1 Shared Epitope (SE) alleles.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 228 (Book Page): Table 6.7: Rheumatoid arthritis (anti-CCP Ab positive): DRB1, 1 SE allele (Odds ratio 4), DRB1, 2 SE alleles (Odds ratio 12).

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and diagnostic criteria of Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
front: Which autoantibody is highly specific (>90%) for the diagnosis of Rheumatoid Arthritis?
back: Anti-CCP (Anti-Cyclic Citrullinated Peptide) antibodies.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 231 (Book Page): Table 6.10: CCP (cyclic citrullinated peptides); various citrullinated proteins... Specific for rheumatoid arthritis.

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and diagnostic criteria of Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
front: Which specific HLA alleles are most strongly associated with Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA) susceptibility?
back: HLA-DRB1 alleles, particularly those containing the "shared epitope" (SE) at positions 70–74.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 228 (Book Page): [Rheumatoid arthritis (anti-CCP Ab positive) DRB1, 1 SE allele... SE refers to shared epitope, so called because the susceptibility alleles map to one region of the DRB1 protein (positions 70–74).]

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and diagnostic criteria of Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
front: What is the primary role of IL-17 and Th17 cells in RA pathophysiology?
back: IL-17 recruits leukocytes and promotes chronic inflammation, leading to tissue damage and synovial fibrosis.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 224 (Book Page): [CD4 + T cells... differentiate into Th1 and Th17 effector cells... IL-17 and other cytokines recruit leukocytes, thus promoting inflammation.]

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and diagnostic criteria of Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
front: How does the joint involvement in RA contrast with Osteoarthritis (OA)?
back:
RA: Symmetric polyarthritis of small joints (MCP, PIP) with inflammatory pannus. 
OA: Mechanical degeneration of weight-bearing joints (knees, hips).
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1198 (Book Page): [Table 26.5: OA Primary pathogenic abnormality: Mechanical injury... RA Primary pathogenic abnormality: Autoimmunity... RA Joints involved: Often begins with small joints of fingers; progression leads to multiple joints.]

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and diagnostic criteria of Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
front: A patient with symmetric hand pain has positive Anti-CCP antibodies. What is the significance of this marker?
back: Anti-Cyclic Citrullinated Peptide (ACPA) is highly specific (60–80%) for Rheumatoid Arthritis and suggests an aggressive course.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 231 (Book Page): [Table 6.10: CCP (cyclic citrullinated peptides); various citrullinated proteins 60–80% Positive; Specific for rheumatoid arthritis.]

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and diagnostic criteria of Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
front: Which two major pro-inflammatory cytokines are primary targets for biological therapy in RA?
back: Tumor Necrosis Factor (TNF) and Interleukin-1 (IL-1).
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1198 (Book Page): [Cytokines such as IL-1 and TNF are released by chondrocytes, synoviocytes, fibroblasts, and inflammatory cells and trigger degradative processes.]

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and diagnostic criteria of Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
front: Identify the four key assessment categories for Rheumatoid Arthritis diagnostic criteria.
back:
1. Joint involvement (number/size)
2. Serology (RF/ACPA)
3. Acute-phase reactants (CRP/ESR)
4. Duration of symptoms (>6 weeks).
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1198 (Book Page): [Table 26.5: Various [indicators], including ACPA, rheumatoid factor; severe chronic inflammation; joint fusion (ankylosis).]

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and diagnostic criteria of Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
front: Define 'Pannus' in the context of Rheumatoid Arthritis morphology.
back: A mass of edematous synovium, inflammatory cells, and granulation tissue that erodes articular cartilage and leads to ankylosis.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1198 (Book Page): [Table 26.5: Inflammatory pannus invading and destroying cartilage; severe chronic inflammation; joint fusion (ankylosis).]

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and diagnostic criteria of Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
front: What is Rheumatoid Factor (RF) and is it specific to RA?
back: An autoantibody (usually IgM) against the Fc portion of self-IgG. It is not specific; also found in Sjögren syndrome and older healthy individuals.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 240 (Book Page): [About 75% of [Sjögren] patients have rheumatoid factor (an antibody reactive with self IgG) whether or not coexisting rheumatoid arthritis is present.]

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and diagnostic criteria of Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
front: How does cigarette smoking contribute to the etiology of Rheumatoid Arthritis?
back: It triggers citrullination (chemical modification) of self-antigens, creating neoantigens that bypass immune tolerance in susceptible individuals.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 229 (Book Page): [Smoking is a risk factor for rheumatoid arthritis, perhaps because it leads to chemical modification of self antigens.]

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and diagnostic criteria of Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
front: List three common extra-articular manifestations of Rheumatoid Arthritis.
back:
1. Skin: Rheumatoid nodules
2. Lungs: Interstitial fibrosis
3. Heart: Pericarditis.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 238 (Book Page): [primarily affects the joints, but may also involve extraarticular tissues such as the skin, blood vessels, lungs, and heart.]

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and diagnostic criteria of Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
front: Q: What is the most specific diagnostic serum autoantibody for Rheumatoid Arthritis?
back: Antibodies to cyclic citrullinated peptides (anti-CCP), present in 60-80% of patients.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 231 (Book Page): [Table 6.10] Rheumatoid arthritis: CCP (cyclic citrullinated peptides); various citrullinated proteins. 60–80%. Specific for rheumatoid arthritis.

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and diagnostic criteria of Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
front: Q: Which immune cell type primarily drives the chronic inflammatory response in Rheumatoid Arthritis?
back: CD4+ helper T cells (specifically Th1 and Th17 subsets) activate macrophages and fibroblasts via cytokines like IFN-̳ and IL-17.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 230 (Book Page): In some autoimmune diseases, such as rheumatoid arthritis, both antibodies and T cell–mediated inflammation may be involved. Page 224 (Book Page): [Table 6.6] Diseases Mediated by T Cells: Rheumatoid arthritis.

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and diagnostic criteria of Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
front: Q: Contrast the primary pathological driver of Rheumatoid Arthritis with Osteoarthritis.
back: RA is driven by autoimmunity and T-cell mediated inflammation. OA is driven by mechanical injury to articular cartilage.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1198 (Book Page): [Table 26.5] Rheumatoid Arthritis: Primary pathogenic abnormality: Autoimmunity; Osteoarthritis: Primary pathogenic abnormality: Mechanical injury to articular cartilage.

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and diagnostic criteria of Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
front: Q: What morphological structure causes the irreversible joint destruction and ankylosis seen in RA?
back: Inflammatory pannus: a mass of edematous synovium and granulation tissue that erodes articular cartilage and bone.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1198 (Book Page): [Table 26.5] Rheumatoid Arthritis: Pathology: Inflammatory pannus invading and destroying cartilage; severe chronic inflammation; joint fusion (ankylosis).

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and diagnostic criteria of Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
front: Q: Which non-HLA gene polymorphism is most frequently associated with increased risk of Rheumatoid Arthritis?
back: PTPN22. It encodes a tyrosine phosphatase that regulates lymphocyte signaling and dampens overactive kinase activity.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 228 (Book Page): Polymorphisms in a gene called PTPN22... are associated with rheumatoid arthritis... PTPN22 is said to be the non-HLA gene that is most frequently implicated in autoimmunity.

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and diagnostic criteria of Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
front: Q: List the characteristic distribution of joint involvement in Rheumatoid Arthritis patients.
back: Typically involves small joints of the fingers (PIP/MCP) and feet first, progressing to larger weight-bearing joints.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1198 (Book Page): [Table 26.5] Rheumatoid Arthritis: Joints involved: Often begins with small joints of fingers; progression leads to multiple joints involved.

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and diagnostic criteria of Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
front: Q: Explain why smoking is considered a major environmental risk factor for Rheumatoid Arthritis.
back: Smoking may trigger chemical modifications (citrullination) of self-antigens, creating neoantigens the immune system no longer tolerates.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 229 (Book Page): Smoking is a risk factor for rheumatoid arthritis, perhaps because it leads to chemical modification of self antigens. Page 231 (Book Page): CCP (cyclic citrullinated peptides).

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and diagnostic criteria of Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
front: Q: Distinguish the joint morphology of RA from SLE based on deformity potential.
back: RA causes erosive synovitis with joint deformity/fusion. SLE joint involvement is nonerosive with minimal deformity.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 235 (Book Page): [SLE] Joint involvement is typically a nonerosive synovitis with little deformity, which contrasts with rheumatoid arthritis.

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and diagnostic criteria of Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
front: Q: Describe the biochemical definition of Rheumatoid Factor (RF).
back: An autoantibody (typically IgM) that reacts with the Fc portion of the patient's own IgG.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 239 (Book Page): rheumatoid factor (an antibody reactive with self IgG). Page 231 (Book Page): [Table 6.10] Rheumatoid factor (not specific) 60–70%.

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and diagnostic criteria of Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
front: Q: Identify three common extra-articular manifestations of Rheumatoid Arthritis.
back:
1. Skin (rheumatoid nodules)
2. Lungs (interstitial fibrosis)
3. Heart/Blood vessels (vasculitis, pericarditis).
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 238 (Book Page): primarily affects the joints, but may also involve extraarticular tissues such as the skin, blood vessels, lungs, and heart.

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and diagnostic criteria of Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
front: Which two serum autoantibodies are the primary diagnostic markers for Rheumatoid Arthritis?
back:
1. Rheumatoid Factor (RF): Sensitivity 60–70%.
2. Anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide (anti-CCP/ACPA): Sensitivity 60–80%; highly specific for RA.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 231 (Book Page): [Table 6.10] Rheumatoid arthritis: CCP (cyclic citrullinated peptides); various citrullinated proteins 60–80% Specific for rheumatoid arthritis; Rheumatoid factor (not specific) 60–70%.

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and diagnostic criteria of Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
front: What is the primary immunologic driver of tissue damage in Rheumatoid Arthritis?
back: A combination of T cell-mediated inflammation (specifically Th1 and Th17 responses) and pathogenic autoantibodies that target joint and systemic antigens.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 230 (Book Page): In some autoimmune diseases, such as rheumatoid arthritis, both antibodies and T cell–mediated inflammation may be involved.

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and diagnostic criteria of Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
front: Contrast the hallmark joint pathology of Rheumatoid Arthritis with Osteoarthritis.
back:
RA: Inflammatory pannus, chronic synovitis, and joint fusion (ankylosis).
OA: Mechanical cartilage degeneration, subchondral cysts, and bone spurs (osteophytes).
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1198 (Book Page): [Table 26.5] RA: Inflammatory pannus invading and destroying cartilage; severe chronic inflammation; joint fusion (ankylosis). OA: Cartilage degeneration and fragmentation, bone spurs, subchondral cysts.

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and diagnostic criteria of Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
front: List the potential extraarticular manifestations of Rheumatoid Arthritis.
back: RA can involve the skin, blood vessels (vasculitis), lungs (pleuritis, interstitial fibrosis), and heart (pericarditis).
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 238 (Book Page): Rheumatoid arthritis is a chronic inflammatory disease that primarily affects the joints, but may also involve extraarticular tissues such as the skin, blood vessels, lungs, and heart.

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and diagnostic criteria of Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
front: Which HLA alleles are most strongly associated with anti-CCP positive Rheumatoid Arthritis?
back: HLA-DRB1 alleles containing the 'Shared Epitope' (SE). Odds ratios for disease increase from 4 (one allele) to 12 (two alleles).
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 228 (Book Page): [Table 6.7] Rheumatoid arthritis (anti-CCP Ab positive): DRB1, 1 SE allele (Odds Ratio 4); DRB1, 2 SE alleles (Odds Ratio 12). SE refers to shared epitope.

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and diagnostic criteria of Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
front: Define the 'Pannus' seen in Rheumatoid Arthritis morphology.
back: A mass of edematous synovium containing proliferating synoviocytes, inflammatory cells, and granulation tissue that invades and erodes articular cartilage.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1198 (Book Page): [Table 26.5] RA: Inflammatory pannus invading and destroying cartilage.

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and diagnostic criteria of Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
front: What non-HLA gene polymorphism is most frequently implicated in RA development?
back: PTPN22. It encodes a tyrosine phosphatase that normally dampens lymphocyte signaling; defective variants lead to excessive, uncontrolled immune responses.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 228 (Book Page): Polymorphisms in a gene called PTPN22... are associated with rheumatoid arthritis... PTPN22 is said to be the non-HLA gene that is most frequently implicated in autoimmunity.

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and diagnostic criteria of Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
front: How does initial joint distribution differ between Rheumatoid Arthritis and Osteoarthritis?
back:
RA: Symmetric involvement, often beginning in small joints (fingers).
OA: Typically affects large weight-bearing joints (knees, hips).
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1198 (Book Page): [Table 26.5] RA: Often begins with small joints of fingers. OA: Primarily weight bearing (knees, hips).

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and diagnostic criteria of Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
front: What is the proposed link between smoking and the pathogenesis of RA?
back: Smoking may trigger 'citrullination' (chemical modification) of self-antigens, creating neoantigens that bypass self-tolerance in genetically predisposed individuals.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 229 (Book Page): Smoking is a risk factor for rheumatoid arthritis, perhaps because it leads to chemical modification of self antigens... [Page 227 (Book Page)] structural changes in these antigens resulting from posttranslational enzymatic modifications.

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and diagnostic criteria of Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
front: Why is Rheumatoid Arthritis categorized as a systemic autoimmune disease?
back: Because the autoimmune reactions are directed against widespread antigens rather than a single organ, resulting in multisystemic lesions (joints, lungs, heart).
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 224 (Book Page): [Diseases] are against widespread antigens, resulting in systemic disease. [Table 6.6] Systemic: Rheumatoid arthritis.

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and diagnostic criteria of Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
front: Which HLA allele is most strongly associated with the development of Rheumatoid Arthritis?
back: HLA-DRB1 (specifically the Shared Epitope alleles).
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 228 (Book Page): [Rheumatoid arthritis (anti-CCP Ab positive) DRB1, 1 SE allele]

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and diagnostic criteria of Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
front: Which CD4+ T-cell subsets are the primary mediators of tissue damage in Rheumatoid Arthritis?
back: Th1 and Th17 cells.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 230 (Book Page): [Most chronic inflammatory diseases are caused by abnormal and excessive Th1 and Th17 responses; examples of these diseases include... rheumatoid arthritis.]

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and diagnostic criteria of Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
front: Contrast the diagnostic specificity of Anti-CCP antibodies versus Rheumatoid Factor in RA diagnosis.
back:
Anti-CCP: High specificity (60-80% of patients).
Rheumatoid Factor: Lower specificity; found in other autoimmune/infectious diseases.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 231 (Book Page): [CCP (cyclic citrullinated peptides)... Specific for rheumatoid arthritis... Rheumatoid factor (not specific)]

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and diagnostic criteria of Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
front: Patient has symmetric finger pain and synovial mass eroding joint cartilage. Name this characteristic morphology.
back: Pannus (an inflammatory mass of synovium, inflammatory cells, and granulation tissue).
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1198 (Book Page): [Inflammatory pannus invading and destroying cartilage; severe chronic inflammation]

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and diagnostic criteria of Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
front: How does smoking contribute to the etiology and chemical pathogenesis of Rheumatoid Arthritis?
back: Promotes chemical modification (citrullination) of self-proteins, creating neoantigens.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 229 (Book Page): [Smoking is a risk factor for rheumatoid arthritis, perhaps because it leads to chemical modification of self antigens.]

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and diagnostic criteria of Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
front: What is the typical joint distribution pattern in early Rheumatoid Arthritis?
back: Symmetric involvement of small joints (e.g., PIP and MCP joints of the fingers).
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1198 (Book Page): [Often begins with small joints of fingers; progression leads to multiple joints involved]

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and diagnostic criteria of Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
front: Define the biochemical nature of Rheumatoid Factor (RF).
back: An autoantibody (usually IgM) reactive with the Fc portion of self-IgG.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 239 (Book Page): [rheumatoid factor (an antibody reactive with self IgG)]

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and diagnostic criteria of Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
front: Contrast the primary target tissue of Rheumatoid Arthritis vs. Osteoarthritis.
back:
RA: Synovium (autoimmune inflammation).
OA: Articular cartilage (mechanical injury).
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1198 (Book Page): [Primary pathogenic abnormality RA: Autoimmunity... OA: Mechanical injury to articular cartilage]

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and diagnostic criteria of Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
front: What pathological end-stage result is characterized by permanent joint fusion in RA?
back: Ankylosis (fibrous or bony fusion of the joint).
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1198 (Book Page): [joint fusion (ankylosis)]

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and diagnostic criteria of Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
front: Which non-HLA gene polymorphism is most frequently implicated in Rheumatoid Arthritis susceptibility?
back: PTPN22 (encodes a protein tyrosine phosphatase).
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 228 (Book Page): [Polymorphisms in a gene called PTPN22... are associated with rheumatoid arthritis]

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and diagnostic criteria of Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
front: Q: Which serological markers are most specific and diagnostic for Rheumatoid Arthritis according to recent clinical criteria?
back: - Anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide (anti-CCP) antibodies (60-80% positive, highly specific). - Rheumatoid Factor (60-70% positive, less specific).
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 231 (Book Page): [CCP (cyclic citrullinated peptides); various citrullinated proteins: 60-80% Specific for rheumatoid arthritis; Rheumatoid factor (not specific) 60-70%]

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and diagnostic criteria of Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
front: Q: What is the primary immunopathologic mechanism and the characteristic morphological hallmark of joint destruction in Rheumatoid Arthritis?
back: - Mechanism: CD4+ T-cell (Th1 and Th17) mediated autoimmunity causing chronic inflammation. - Morphology: Formation of inflammatory pannus (granulation tissue) that invades cartilage and bone, potentially causing ankylosis (joint fusion).
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1198 (Book Page): [Primary pathogenic abnormality: Autoimmunity. Pathology: Inflammatory pannus invading and destroying cartilage; severe chronic inflammation; joint fusion (ankylosis).]

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and diagnostic criteria of Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
front: Which HLA-DRB1 genetic component is most strongly associated with Rheumatoid Arthritis susceptibility?
back: The 'Shared Epitope' (SE), representing specific alleles mapping to positions 70–74 of the DRB1 protein.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 228 (Book Page): [SE refers to shared epitope, so called because the susceptibility alleles map to one region of the DRB1 protein (positions 70–74).]

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and diagnostic criteria of Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
front: What is the primary T-cell mediated pathophysiological mechanism in Rheumatoid Arthritis?
back: Excessive Th1 and Th17 responses releasing cytokines (TNF, IL-17) that drive chronic synovial inflammation and tissue destruction.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 230 (Book Page): [Most chronic inflammatory diseases are caused by abnormal and excessive Th1 and Th17 responses; examples of these diseases include... rheumatoid arthritis.]

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and diagnostic criteria of Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
front: Contrast the joint involvement patterns of Rheumatoid Arthritis versus Osteoarthritis.
back: RA: Symmetrical, predominantly small joints (MCP, PIP). OA: Asymmetrical, predominantly weight-bearing joints (hips, knees).
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1198 (Book Page): [Osteoarthritis: Primarily weight bearing (knees, hips). Rheumatoid Arthritis: Often begins with small joints of fingers; progression leads to multiple joints involved.]

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and diagnostic criteria of Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
front: A middle-aged female presents with symmetrical MCP swelling and 90 minutes of morning stiffness. Diagnosis?
back: Rheumatoid Arthritis (key features: symmetrical small joint involvement, morning stiffness >1 hour).
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1198 (Book Page): [Rheumatoid Arthritis... often begins with small joints of fingers; progression leads to multiple joints involved; joint fusion (ankylosis).]

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and diagnostic criteria of Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
front: Why is anti-TNF therapy a cornerstone in Rheumatoid Arthritis management?
back: TNF is a primary inflammatory mediator in RA; its inhibition stops leukocyte recruitment and synovial cell protease production.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 238 (Book Page): [anti-TNF therapy, which is effective in rheumatoid arthritis and other autoimmune diseases...]

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and diagnostic criteria of Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
front: Which specific serum autoantibody is highly specific for the diagnosis of Rheumatoid Arthritis?
back: Anti-Cyclic Citrullinated Peptide (Anti-CCP) antibodies (also known as ACPA).
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 231 (Book Page): [Rheumatoid arthritis: CCP (cyclic citrullinated peptides); various citrullinated proteins (60–80% positive). Specific for rheumatoid arthritis.]

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and diagnostic criteria of Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
front: Define 'Pannus' in the context of Rheumatoid Arthritis morphology.
back: A proliferative mass of inflamed synovium, fibroblasts, and granulation tissue that invades and erodes articular cartilage.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1198 (Book Page): [Pathology: Inflammatory pannus invading and destroying cartilage; severe chronic inflammation; joint fusion (ankylosis).]

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and diagnostic criteria of Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
front: How does joint deformity in Systemic Lupus Erythematosus differ from Rheumatoid Arthritis?
back: RA: Erosive and deforming. SLE: Nonerosive synovitis with minimal deformity.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 235 (Book Page): [Joints. Joint involvement is typically a nonerosive synovitis with little deformity, which contrasts with rheumatoid arthritis.]

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and diagnostic criteria of Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
front: What environmental trigger is linked to RA through the modification of self-antigens (citrullination)?
back: Smoking; it is thought to induce chemical modification of proteins, creating neoantigens (citrullinated proteins).
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 229 (Book Page): [Smoking is a risk factor for rheumatoid arthritis, perhaps because it leads to chemical modification of self antigens.]

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and diagnostic criteria of Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)
front: What is the ultimate morphological consequence of severe, untreated chronic Rheumatoid Arthritis?
back: Ankylosis (joint fusion), which can be fibrous or eventually bony, leading to total loss of movement.
