coreConcept: Radiological Findings of Metastatic Bone Disease
front: Which specific cancers typically produce blastic vs. lytic skeletal metastases in adults?
back: Prostate cancer is predominantly blastic. Kidney, lung, and GI tract cancers predominantly produce lytic (bone-destroying) lesions.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1197 (Book Page): prostatic adenocarcinoma is predominantly blastic, whereas carcinomas of the kidney, lung, and gastrointestinal tract and malignant melanoma produce lytic lesions.

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and radiological findings of bone, cartilaginous and soft tumors
front: Q: What is the classic clinical presentation and pharmacological relief for Osteoid Osteoma?
back:
- Severe nocturnal pain.
- Rapidly relieved by aspirin or NSAIDs (due to PGE2 production).
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1189 (Book Page): [osteoid osteomas present with severe nocturnal pain that is probably caused by prostaglandin E 2 (PGE 2) produced by the proliferating osteoblasts and is relieved by aspirin and other NSAIDs.]

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and radiological findings of bone, cartilaginous and soft tumors
front: Q: Identify the bimodal age peaks and the most common anatomical site for Osteosarcoma.
back:
- Age: 75% occur <20 years; secondary peak in elderly.
- Site: Metaphysis of long bones, specifically the knee (distal femur/proximal tibia).
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1189 (Book Page): [The age distribution of osteosarcoma is bimodal, with 75% occurring before 20 years of age... almost 50% are near the knee in the distal femur or proximal tibia.]

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and radiological findings of bone, cartilaginous and soft tumors
front: Q: Describe the pathognomonic radiological 'Codman triangle' seen in Osteosarcoma.
back:
- Triangular shadow between the bone cortex and raised periosteum.
- Indicates an aggressive tumor lifting the periosteum.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1189 (Book Page): [The triangular shadow between the cortex and raised periosteal ends, known radiographically as a Codman triangle, indicates an aggressive tumor.]

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and radiological findings of bone, cartilaginous and soft tumors
front: Q: What are the two most common germline mutations predisposing to Osteosarcoma?
back:
- RB mutations (Retinoblastoma patients).
- TP53 mutations (Li-Fraumeni syndrome).
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1189 (Book Page): [RB mutations are present in up to 70% of sporadic osteosarcomas; germline RB mutations confer a 1000-fold increased risk... TP53 is mutated in the germline of individuals with Li-Fraumeni syndrome.]

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and radiological findings of bone, cartilaginous and soft tumors
front: Q: Define the morphological hallmark required for a definitive diagnosis of Osteosarcoma.
back: - Presence of malignant tumor cells directly producing unmineralized osteoid or mineralized bone.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1190 (Book Page): [Diagnosis of osteosarcoma requires the presence of malignant tumor cells producing unmineralized osteoid or mineralized bone.]

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and radiological findings of bone, cartilaginous and soft tumors
front: Q: What defines the morphological relationship between an Osteochondroma and its host bone?
back:
- Bony stalk capped by hyaline cartilage.
- Medullary cavity of the tumor is continuous with the medullary cavity of the host bone.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1191 (Book Page): [The cortex of the stalk merges with the cortex of the host bone, so that the medullary cavity of the osteochondroma is in continuity with that of the bone from which it arises.]

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and radiological findings of bone, cartilaginous and soft tumors
front: Q: Contrast the typical anatomical distribution of Chondrosarcoma versus Enchondroma.
back:
- Chondrosarcoma: Axial skeleton (pelvis, shoulder, ribs).
- Enchondroma: Distal extremities (small bones of hands and feet).
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1192 (Book Page): [Chondrosarcomas commonly arise in the axial skeleton, especially the pelvis, shoulder, and ribs, but, unlike benign enchondroma, distal extremities are rarely involved.]

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and radiological findings of bone, cartilaginous and soft tumors
front: Q: What is the pathognomonic genetic translocation and microscopic appearance of Ewing Sarcoma?
back:
- Genetics: t(11;22) translocation (EWSR1/FLI1 fusion).
- Microscopy: Sheets of uniform, small, round blue cells with scant glycogen-rich cytoplasm.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1193 (Book Page): [Greater than 90% of Ewing sarcomas contain a balanced translocation involving the EWSR1 gene... partner is the FLI1 gene... uniform small, round cells with scant cytoplasm that may be clear due to abundant glycogen.]

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and radiological findings of bone, cartilaginous and soft tumors
front: Q: Explain the role of RANKL in the pathophysiology of Giant Cell Tumor (GCT).
back:
- Neoplastic osteoblast precursors overexpress RANKL.
- This stimulates massive differentiation of non-neoplastic osteoclast precursors, causing destructive bone resorption.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1194 (Book Page): [neoplastic cells are primitive osteoblast precursors that express high levels of RANKL, which in turn promotes the proliferation of osteoclast precursors and their differentiation into mature osteoclasts.]

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and radiological findings of bone, cartilaginous and soft tumors
coreConcept: Aneurysmal Bone Cyst Radiology and Morphology
front: Q: Clinical Case: 15-year-old with a tibial lesion showing 'soap bubble' appearance and air-fluid levels on CT.
back:
- Diagnosis: Aneurysmal Bone Cyst (ABC).
- Key Feature: Multiloculated blood-filled cystic spaces separated by fibrous septa.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1195 (Book Page): [trabeculae may create a “soap bubble” appearance... air-fluid levels by computed tomography... ABCs consist of multiple blood-filled cystic spaces separated by thin, tan-white septa.]

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and radiological findings of bone, cartilaginous and soft tumors
front: Q: What is a 'Codman triangle' and which aggressive bone tumor does it typically signify?
back: A: A triangular shadow between the cortex and raised periosteal ends. It signifies an aggressive tumor, most characteristically Osteosarcoma.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1189 (Book Page): The triangular shadow between the cortex and raised periosteal ends, known radiographically as a Codman triangle, indicates an aggressive tumor.

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and radiological findings of bone, cartilaginous and soft tumors
front: Q: Describe the genetic etiology and signaling disruption associated with Osteochondroma.
back:
A: • Loss-of-function mutations in EXT1/EXT2 genes.
• Defective heparan sulfate synthesis disrupts Hedgehog signaling (Indian hedgehog) in the growth plate.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1191 (Book Page): Hereditary exostoses are associated with germline loss-of-function mutations in either the EXT1 or the EXT2 gene... disrupting Hedgehog signaling and chondrocyte differentiation.

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and radiological findings of bone, cartilaginous and soft tumors
front: Q: Contrast Osteoid Osteoma and Osteoblastoma based on size and response to NSAIDs.
back:
A: • Osteoid Osteoma: <2cm; pain relieved by aspirin (PGE2 mediated).
• Osteoblastoma: >2cm; involves posterior spine; pain unresponsive to aspirin.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1189 (Book Page): osteoid osteomas are less than 2 cm... relieved by aspirin... Osteoblastomas are larger than 2 cm... cause pain that is unresponsive to aspirin.

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and radiological findings of bone, cartilaginous and soft tumors
front: Q: A 12-year-old child presents with a painful thigh, fever, and 'onion-skin' periosteal reaction. Diagnosis?
back: A: Ewing Sarcoma. Key features: Diaphyseal location, primitive small round cells (histology), and systemic symptoms mimicking infection.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1193 (Book Page): Ewing sarcoma usually arises in the diaphysis of long tubular bones... periosteal reaction produces layers of reactive bone deposited in an onion-skin fashion.

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and radiological findings of bone, cartilaginous and soft tumors
front: Q: Explain the cellular pathophysiology of Giant Cell Tumor (Osteoclastoma).
back: A: Neoplastic osteoblast precursors overexpress RANKL. This drives non-neoplastic osteoclast precursors to differentiate into mature osteoclasts, causing destructive bone resorption.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1194 (Book Page): The neoplastic cells are primitive osteoblast precursors that express high levels of RANKL, which in turn promotes the proliferation of osteoclast precursors.

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and radiological findings of bone, cartilaginous and soft tumors
front: Q: Identify the characteristic chromosomal translocation and fusion gene in Ewing Sarcoma.
back:
A: • t(11;22)(q24;q12).
• Results in the EWSR1/FLI1 fusion gene, which acts as a dysregulated transcription factor.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1193 (Book Page): Greater than 90% of Ewing sarcomas contain a balanced translocation involving the EWSR1 gene on chromosome 22... FLI1 gene on chromosome 11, creating an EWSR1/FLI1 fusion gene.

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and radiological findings of bone, cartilaginous and soft tumors
front: Q: How do IDH1/IDH2 mutations facilitate the development of Chondromas?
back: A: Mutations produce 'oncometabolite' 2-hydroxyglutarate, which interferes with DNA methylation and induces oncogenic epigenetic changes (transformation by association).
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1192 (Book Page): IDH mutations... lead to the synthesis of 2-hydroxyglutarate. This 'oncometabolite' interferes with regulation of DNA methylation... transformation by association.

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and radiological findings of bone, cartilaginous and soft tumors
front: Q: A 55-year-old male presents with a pelvic mass showing 'flocculent densities' on imaging. Likely diagnosis?
back: A: Chondrosarcoma. Characteristics: Axial skeleton (pelvis/shoulder), malignant cartilage production, and flocculent densities representing calcified matrix.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1192 (Book Page): Chondrosarcomas commonly arise in the axial skeleton, especially the pelvis... the calcified matrix of chondrosarcomas appears as foci of flocculent densities.

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and radiological findings of bone, cartilaginous and soft tumors
front: Q: Describe the molecular mechanism behind Aneurysmal Bone Cyst (ABC) formation.
back: A: Rearrangements of USP6 gene (17p13). This up-regulates NF-κB and matrix metalloproteases, leading to cystic bone resorption and blood-filled spaces.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1195 (Book Page): rearrangement results in fusion of the USP6 coding region... regulates the activity of the transcription factor NF-κB... leading to cystic bone resorption.

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and radiological findings of bone, cartilaginous and soft tumors
front: Q: What is the microscopic defining feature required to diagnose Osteosarcoma?
back: A: Malignant tumor cells directly producing unmineralized osteoid or mineralized bone (typically fine and lacelike).
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1190 (Book Page): Diagnosis of osteosarcoma requires the presence of malignant tumor cells producing unmineralized osteoid or mineralized bone.

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and radiological findings of bone, cartilaginous and soft tumors
front: Q: What is the 'Codman triangle' in osteosarcoma radiology?
back: A: A triangular shadow between the cortex and the raised periosteal ends. It indicates an aggressive tumor lifting the periosteum away from the bone.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1189 (Book Page): [The triangular shadow between the cortex and raised periosteal ends, known radiographically as a Codman triangle, indicates an aggressive tumor.]

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and radiological findings of bone, cartilaginous and soft tumors
front: Q: Why does osteoid osteoma cause severe nocturnal pain?
back: A: It is caused by Prostaglandin E2 (PGE2) produced by proliferating osteoblasts. This pain is characteristically relieved by aspirin and other NSAIDs.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1189 (Book Page): [severe nocturnal pain that is probably caused by prostaglandin E 2 (PGE 2 ) produced by the proliferating osteoblasts and is relieved by aspirin and other NSAIDs.]

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and radiological findings of bone, cartilaginous and soft tumors
front: Q: Contrast osteoid osteoma and osteoblastoma regarding size and symptom relief.
back:
A: 
- Osteoid osteoma: <2 cm; relieved by aspirin.
- Osteoblastoma: >2 cm; pain is unresponsive to aspirin.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1189 (Book Page): [By definition, osteoid osteomas are less than 2 cm in diameter... relieved by aspirin... Osteoblastomas are larger than 2 cm... cause pain that is unresponsive to aspirin.]

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and radiological findings of bone, cartilaginous and soft tumors
front: Q: What is the genetic hallmark and classic periosteal reaction in Ewing Sarcoma?
back:
A: 
- Genetic: t(11;22) translocation creating EWSR1/FLI1 fusion.
- Radiology: 'Onion-skin' appearance of reactive bone layers.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1193 (Book Page): [rearrangements are present... t(11;22) involving the EWSR1 gene... characteristic periosteal reaction produces layers of reactive bone deposited in an onion-skin fashion.]

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and radiological findings of bone, cartilaginous and soft tumors
front: Q: What is the pharmacological rationale for using Denosumab in Giant Cell Tumors?
back: A: Denosumab is a RANKL inhibitor. It targets the high levels of RANKL expressed by neoplastic osteoblast precursors, stopping destructive osteoclast recruitment.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1194 (Book Page): [The neoplastic cells are primitive osteoblast precursors that express high levels of RANKL... The RANKL inhibitor denosumab has shown promise as an adjuvant therapy.]

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and radiological findings of bone, cartilaginous and soft tumors
front: Q: State the mandatory microscopic feature for the diagnosis of Osteosarcoma.
back: A: The presence of malignant tumor cells directly producing unmineralized osteoid or mineralized bone, often in a fine, lace-like pattern.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1190 (Book Page): [Diagnosis of osteosarcoma requires the presence of malignant tumor cells producing unmineralized osteoid or mineralized bone, which is typically fine and lacelike.]

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and radiological findings of bone, cartilaginous and soft tumors
front: Q: Describe the etiology of multiple hereditary exostosis syndrome (Osteochondroma).
back: A: Germline loss-of-function mutations in EXT1 or EXT2 genes. This disrupts heparan sulfate glycosaminoglycan synthesis and hedgehog signaling in chondrocytes.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1191 (Book Page): [Hereditary exostoses are associated with germline loss-of-function mutations in either the EXT1 or the EXT2 gene... disrupting Hedgehog signaling and chondrocyte differentiation.]

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and radiological findings of bone, cartilaginous and soft tumors
front: Q: A 50-year-old male presents with a large pelvic mass showing 'flocculent' densities on X-ray. Diagnosis?
back: A: Chondrosarcoma. Key clues: Age (>40), axial skeleton location (pelvis), and characteristic calcified flocculent densities on imaging.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1192 (Book Page): [Chondrosarcomas commonly arise in the axial skeleton, especially the pelvis... On imaging, the calcified matrix of chondrosarcomas appears as foci of flocculent densities.]

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and radiological findings of bone, cartilaginous and soft tumors
front: Q: What biochemical mechanism drives the 'Ground Glass' appearance in Fibrous Dysplasia?
back: A: Somatic gain-of-function GNAS1 mutations. These cause constitutively active Gs-alpha, increasing cAMP, promoting proliferation, and arresting osteoblast maturation.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1196 (Book Page): [All forms of fibrous dysplasia result from somatic gain-of-function mutations in GNAS1... constitutively active G s protein promotes cellular proliferation and disturbs osteoblast differentiation.]

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and radiological findings of bone, cartilaginous and soft tumors
front: Q: Which anatomical site and region is most commonly affected by adolescent Osteosarcoma?
back: A: The metaphyseal region of long bones, with nearly 50% of cases occurring near the knee (distal femur or proximal tibia).
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1189 (Book Page): [tumors usually arise in the metaphyseal region of the long bones; almost 50% are near the knee in the distal femur or proximal tibia.]

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and radiological findings of bone, cartilaginous and soft tumors
front: Q: Differentiate Osteoid Osteoma from Osteoblastoma based on size and anatomical predilection.
back:
• Osteoid Osteoma: <2 cm; prefers appendicular skeleton (femur/tibia cortex).
• Osteoblastoma: >2 cm; prefers posterior elements of the vertebral column (laminae/pedicles).
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1189 (Book Page): [By definition, osteoid osteomas are less than 2 cm in diameter... about 50% involving the cortex of the femur or tibia. Osteoblastomas are larger than 2 cm, typically involve the posterior spine.]

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and radiological findings of bone, cartilaginous and soft tumors
front: Q: Which tumor suppressor gene mutations are most frequently implicated in sporadic Osteosarcoma?
back:
• RB mutations (found in up to 70% of cases).
• TP53 mutations (germline link in Li-Fraumeni syndrome).
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1189 (Book Page): [RB mutations are present in up to 70% of sporadic osteosarcomas; germline RB mutations confer a 1000-fold increased risk... TP53 is mutated in the germline of individuals with Li-Fraumeni syndrome.]

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and radiological findings of bone, cartilaginous and soft tumors
front: Q: Describe the radiological significance of a 'Codman Triangle' in Osteosarcoma.
back:
• Definition: A triangular shadow between the cortex and raised periosteal ends.
• Indication: Signifies an aggressive tumor lifting the periosteum followed by reactive bone formation.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1189 (Book Page): [The triangular shadow between the cortex and raised periosteal ends, known radiographically as a Codman triangle, indicates an aggressive tumor.]

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and radiological findings of bone, cartilaginous and soft tumors
front: Q: A 15-year-old presents with a distal femur mass. X-ray shows a 'sunburst' pattern. Diagnosis?
back:
• Diagnosis: Osteosarcoma.
• Pathophysiology: Malignant cells producing unmineralized osteoid or mineralized woven bone, lifting the periosteum.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1189 (Book Page)-1190: [Osteosarcoma incidence peaks during adolescence... destructive, mixed lytic and blastic mass... malignant cells producing woven bone.]

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and radiological findings of bone, cartilaginous and soft tumors
front: Q: Describe the characteristic morphological features of an Osteochondroma (Exostosis).
back:
• Bony stalk (pedunculated or sessile) with a hyaline cartilage cap.
• Medullary cavity of the stalk is continuous with the host bone medullary cavity.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1191 (Book Page): [The cortex of the stalk merges with the cortex of the host bone, so that the medullary cavity of the osteochondroma is in continuity with that of the bone from which it arises.]

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and radiological findings of bone, cartilaginous and soft tumors
front: Q: Explain the 'transformation by association' mechanism in syndromic Enchondromas (Ollier Disease).
back:
• Mutant IDH1/IDH2 cells produce the 'oncometabolite' 2-hydroxyglutarate.
• This diffuses into normal neighboring cells, causing oncogenic epigenetic changes (DNA methylation).
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1192 (Book Page): [2-hydroxyglutarate produced by IDH-mutated cells diffuses into neighboring cells... causing oncogenic epigenetic changes in genetically normal neighbors... 'transformation by association.']

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and radiological findings of bone, cartilaginous and soft tumors
front: Q: State the diagnostic chromosomal translocation and fusion gene for Ewing Sarcoma.
back:
• Translocation: t(11;22)(q24;q12).
• Fusion Gene: EWSR1/FLI1 (fusion creates a chimeric protein dysregulating transcription).
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1193 (Book Page): [Greater than 90% of Ewing sarcomas contain a balanced translocation involving the EWSR1 gene on chromosome 22... the other partner is the FLI1 gene on chromosome 11.]

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and radiological findings of bone, cartilaginous and soft tumors
front: Q: Describe the microscopic morphology of a Giant Cell Tumor (Osteoclastoma).
back:
• Uniform oval mononuclear neoplastic cells (osteoblast precursors).
• Abundant multinucleated osteoclast-type giant cells (containing 100+ nuclei).
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1194 (Book Page): [Histologically, the tumors consist of uniform oval mononuclear tumor cells and abundant osteoclast-type giant cells with 100 or more nuclei.]

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and radiological findings of bone, cartilaginous and soft tumors
front: Q: What is the triad of McCune-Albright Syndrome associated with Fibrous Dysplasia?
back:
• Polyostotic Fibrous Dysplasia.
• Café-au-lait skin pigmentations (serpiginous borders).
• Endocrine abnormalities (e.g., precocious puberty).
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1196 (Book Page): [McCune-Albright syndrome: polyostotic disease, associated with café-au-lait skin pigmentations and endocrine abnormalities, especially precocious puberty.]

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and radiological findings of bone, cartilaginous and soft tumors
front: Q: Compare the mechanism of Osteoblastic vs. Osteolytic skeletal metastases.
back:
• Osteoblastic: Tumor cells (Prostate) secrete WNT proteins to stimulate bone formation.
• Osteolytic: Tumor cells (Lung/Kidney) secrete PTHrP to upregulate RANKL, activating osteoclasts.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1197 (Book Page): [Prostatic adenocarcinoma is predominantly blastic... Sclerotic metastases may result from tumor cells secreting WNT proteins... lytic lesions... up-regulate RANKL on osteoblasts.]

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and radiological findings of bone, cartilaginous and soft tumors
coreConcept: Biochemical basis of Osteoid Osteoma pain
front: Q: Which metabolite is responsible for the nocturnal pain in Osteoid Osteoma that is relieved by aspirin?
back: Prostaglandin E2 (PGE2).
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1189 (Book Page): [nocturnal pain that is probably caused by prostaglandin E 2 (PGE 2) produced by the proliferating osteoblasts and is relieved by aspirin]

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and radiological findings of bone, cartilaginous and soft tumors
front: Q: List the two primary tumor suppressor gene mutations most commonly associated with sporadic Osteosarcoma.
back: - RB mutations (up to 70%); - TP53 mutations.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1189 (Book Page): [RB mutations are present in up to 70% of sporadic osteosarcomas; TP53 is mutated in the germline... Abnormalities that interfere with p53 function are common in sporadic osteosarcomas.]

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and radiological findings of bone, cartilaginous and soft tumors
front: Q: Contrast the radiographic hallmark of Osteosarcoma with the central feature of an Osteoid Osteoma.
back: - Osteosarcoma: Codman triangle (reactive periosteal bone); - Osteoid Osteoma: Nidus (radiolucent core).
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1189 (Book Page): [triangular shadow between the cortex and raised periosteal ends, known radiographically as a Codman triangle... nidus, which forms a small radiolucent core]

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and radiological findings of bone, cartilaginous and soft tumors
front: Q: A 12-year-old male presents with fever and 'onion-skin' periosteal reaction on femur. Name the diagnosis and genetic translocation.
back: - Diagnosis: Ewing Sarcoma; - Translocation: t(11;22) involving EWSR1 and FLI1 genes.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1193 (Book Page): [Ewing sarcoma... onion-skin fashion... Greater than 90% of Ewing sarcomas contain a balanced translocation involving the EWSR1 gene on chromosome 22... FLI1 gene on chromosome 11]

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and radiological findings of bone, cartilaginous and soft tumors
front: Q: What is the molecular driver of bone resorption in Giant Cell Tumors, and which drug targets it?
back: - Driver: Neoplastic cells express RANKL; - Drug: Denosumab (RANKL inhibitor).
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1194 (Book Page): [neoplastic cells... express high levels of RANKL, which in turn promotes the proliferation of osteoclast precursors... RANKL inhibitor denosumab has shown promise]

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and radiological findings of bone, cartilaginous and soft tumors
front: Q: Define the macroscopic defining feature of an Osteochondroma (Exostosis).
back: A bony stalk (pedunculated or sessile) capped by benign hyaline cartilage.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1190 (Book Page): [attached to the skeleton by a bony stalk capped by cartilage.]

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and radiological findings of bone, cartilaginous and soft tumors
front: Q: Name the syndrome involving polyostotic fibrous dysplasia, café-au-lait spots, and precocious puberty.
back: - McCune-Albright Syndrome (caused by somatic GNAS1 mutation).
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1196 (Book Page): [McCune-Albright syndrome: polyostotic disease, associated with café-au-lait skin pigmentations and endocrine abnormalities... gain-of-function mutations in GNAS1]

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and radiological findings of bone, cartilaginous and soft tumors
front: Q: Differentiate the prognosis and metastatic potential of Grade 1 versus Grade 3 Chondrosarcoma.
back: - Grade 1: 80-90% survival; rarely metastasizes; - Grade 3: 43% survival; 70% hematogenous spread (to lungs).
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1193 (Book Page): [Most conventional chondrosarcomas are grade 1... 5-year survival rates of 80% to 90%... 70% of grade 3 tumors spread hematogenously... 5-year survival is only 43%.]

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and radiological findings of bone, cartilaginous and soft tumors
front: Q: Explain the mechanism by which lytic bone metastases (e.g. from lung) induce bone resorption.
back: Tumor cells secrete PTHrP/cytokines to up-regulate RANKL on osteoblasts, which activates osteoclasts.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1197 (Book Page): [Tumor cells... secrete substances such as... PTHrP that up-regulate RANKL on osteoblasts and stromal cells, thereby stimulating osteoclast activity.]

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and radiological findings of bone, cartilaginous and soft tumors
front: Q: Describe the characteristic 'soap bubble' radiological finding associated with which expansile cystic lesion?
back: Aneurysmal Bone Cyst (ABC).
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1195 (Book Page): [trabeculae may create a 'soap bubble' appearance... internal septae with air-fluid levels... blood-filled cystic spaces separated by thin, tan-white septa.]

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and diagnostic criteria of Crystal Arthritis (Gout/Pseudogout)
front: Q: What is the primary biochemical requirement for the diagnosis of Gout?
back: Hyperuricemia, defined as a plasma urate level exceeding 6.8 mg/dL, which is the limit of solubility at core body temperature.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1230 (Book Page): [Hyperuricemia (plasma urate level > 6.8 mg/dL) is necessary, but not sufficient, for the development of gout.]

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and diagnostic criteria of Crystal Arthritis (Gout/Pseudogout)
front: Q: Describe the role of the NLRP3 inflammasome in the pathophysiology of acute gouty arthritis.
back: Macrophages phagocytose monosodium urate (MSU) crystals, activating the NLRP3 inflammasome, which triggers the release of active IL-1̢, driving acute inflammation.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1231 (Book Page): [MSU crystals are recognized by the NLRP3 inflammasome... leading to the production of IL-1̢, which promotes the accumulation of neutrophils.]

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and diagnostic criteria of Crystal Arthritis (Gout/Pseudogout)
front: Q: Contrast the crystal morphology and birefringence of Gout vs. Pseudogout.
back: Gout: Needle-shaped, strong negative birefringence. Pseudogout: Rhomboid/geometric, weak positive birefringence.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1235 (Book Page): [MSU crystals are needle-shaped and negatively birefringent; CPPD crystals are rhomboid and weakly positively birefringent.]

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and diagnostic criteria of Crystal Arthritis (Gout/Pseudogout)
front: Q: A 50-year-old male presents with excruciating pain and swelling in the first MTP joint after a steak dinner. Diagnosis?
back: Acute Gouty Arthritis (Podagra), likely triggered by a high-purine meal leading to MSU crystal deposition.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1233 (Book Page): [The first metatarsophalangeal joint is involved in 50% of first attacks and eventually is involved in most cases (podagra).]

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and diagnostic criteria of Crystal Arthritis (Gout/Pseudogout)
front: Q: What are the two primary metabolic mechanisms leading to hyperuricemia in gout?
back:
1. Overproduction of uric acid (10% of cases, often enzymatic).
2. Underexcretion of uric acid by the kidneys (90% of cases).
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1231 (Book Page): [Hyperuricemia may result from overproduction or underexcretion of uric acid, or both.]

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and diagnostic criteria of Crystal Arthritis (Gout/Pseudogout)
front: Q: Define the histological hallmarks of a chronic Gouty Tophus.
back: Large crystalline aggregates (urate) surrounded by an intense inflammatory reaction of macrophages, lymphocytes, and foreign-body giant cells.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1233 (Book Page): [Tophi are pathognomonic for gout and consist of large encrustations of urate crystals surrounded by an intense inflammatory reaction.]

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and diagnostic criteria of Crystal Arthritis (Gout/Pseudogout)
front: Q: Why is Pseudogout (CPPD) more common in patients over 50 years of age?
back: Due to age-related changes in articular cartilage and increased pyrophosphate production, with prevalence reaching 30-60% in those over age 85.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1235 (Book Page): [The prevalence of CPPD increases with age, being present in as many as half of those 85 years or older.]

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and diagnostic criteria of Crystal Arthritis (Gout/Pseudogout)
front: Q: In a suspected case of septic arthritis vs. gout, what is the definitive diagnostic procedure?
back: Synovial fluid aspiration and polarized light microscopy to identify the presence and type of crystals.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1234 (Book Page): [A definitive diagnosis of gout requires the identification of MSU crystals in aspirated joint fluid.]

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and diagnostic criteria of Crystal Arthritis (Gout/Pseudogout)
front: Q: Explain the 'HGPRT salvage pathway' defect in the context of gout.
back: HGPRT deficiency prevents recycling of hypoxanthine/guanine, shunting them to uric acid production, leading to severe hyperuricemia (Lesch-Nyhan syndrome).
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1231 (Book Page): [Complete absence of HGPRT results in the Lesch-Nyhan syndrome... partial deficiency may present as gout in young adults.]

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and diagnostic criteria of Crystal Arthritis (Gout/Pseudogout)
front: Q: Name three common extra-articular sites where tophi may develop.
back:
1. External ear (helix/antihelix)
2. Olecranon bursa
3. Achilles tendon
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1233 (Book Page): [Tophi can occur in the articular cartilage, ligaments, tendons, and soft tissues, including the ear lobes.]

category: Classify bone, cartilaginous and soft tumors
front: Q: Classify primary bone-forming tumors based on biological behavior as per UHS standards.
back:
1. Benign: Osteoid osteoma, Osteoblastoma.
2. Malignant: Osteosarcoma.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1188 (Book Page): [Table 26.4: Bone forming (32) Benign: Osteoid osteoma, Osteoblastoma. Malignant: Osteosarcoma]

category: Classify bone, cartilaginous and soft tumors
coreConcept: Diagnostic Distinctions in Benign Bone Tumors
front: Q: Distinguish Osteoid Osteoma from Osteoblastoma based on size and clinical response to aspirin.
back:
- Osteoid Osteoma: < 2 cm; pain relieved by aspirin (NSAIDs).
- Osteoblastoma: > 2 cm; pain unresponsive to aspirin.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1189 (Book Page): [By definition, osteoid osteomas are less than 2 cm... relieved by aspirin... Osteoblastomas are larger than 2 cm... unresponsive to aspirin]

category: Classify bone, cartilaginous and soft tumors
front: Q: Classify cartilaginous tumors into benign and malignant categories.
back:
1. Benign: Osteochondroma, Chondroma (Enchondroma), Chondroblastoma, Chondromyxoid fibroma.
2. Malignant: Chondrosarcoma.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1188 (Book Page): [Table 26.4: Cartilage forming (40) Benign: Osteochondroma, Chondroma, Chondroblastoma, Chondromyxoid fibroma. Malignant: Chondrosarcoma]

category: Classify bone, cartilaginous and soft tumors
front: Q: A 16-year-old presents with a knee mass and 'Codman triangle' on X-ray. Classify this tumor by origin and typical location.
back:
- Tumor: Osteosarcoma (Malignant bone-forming).
- Location: Metaphysis of distal femur or proximal tibia (near growth plate).
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1189 (Book Page): [Osteosarcoma incidence peaks during adolescence... most frequently involves the knee... Codman triangle, indicates an aggressive tumor.]

category: Classify bone, cartilaginous and soft tumors
front: Q: List the four major histological variants used to subclassify Chondrosarcoma.
back:
1. Conventional.
2. Clear cell.
3. Dedifferentiated.
4. Mesenchymal.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1192 (Book Page): [Chondrosarcomas are... subclassified histologically as conventional, clear cell, dedifferentiated, and mesenchymal variants.]

category: Classify bone, cartilaginous and soft tumors
front: Q: Which tumor is specifically classified as being of 'Notochordal origin'?
back: Chordoma (Malignant; typically located in the clivus or sacrum).
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1188 (Book Page): [Table 26.4: Notochordal (5) Malignant: Chordoma. Common Locations: Clivus, sacrum]

category: Classify bone, cartilaginous and soft tumors
front: Q: Classify primary bone tumors of 'Unknown Origin' into their benign and malignant subsets.
back:
1. Benign: Giant cell tumor, Aneurysmal bone cyst (ABC).
2. Malignant: Ewing sarcoma, Adamantinoma.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1188 (Book Page): [Table 26.4: Unknown origin (19) Benign: Giant cell tumor, Aneurysmal bone cyst. Malignant: Ewing sarcoma, Adamantinoma]

category: Classify bone, cartilaginous and soft tumors
front: Q: A child's X-ray shows a 'moth-eaten' lytic lesion in the femoral diaphysis with 'onion-skin' periosteal reaction. Classify the likely tumor.
back: Ewing Sarcoma (Malignant tumor of unknown origin; characterized by small round cells).
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1193 (Book Page): [Ewing sarcoma... Destructive lytic tumor with permeative, or moth-eaten, margins... characteristic periosteal reaction produces layers of reactive bone deposited in an onion-skin fashion.]

category: Classify bone, cartilaginous and soft tumors
front: Q: Classify Osteosarcoma into Primary vs. Secondary based on age and predisposing conditions.
back:
- Primary: Young patients (<20 years); metaphysis.
- Secondary: Older adults; associated with Paget disease, bone infarcts, or prior radiation.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1189 (Book Page): [75% occurring before 20 years of age... smaller peak occurs in older adults... associated with predisposing conditions such as Paget disease, bone infarcts, and prior radiation]

category: Classify bone, cartilaginous and soft tumors
front: Q: What is the most common form of skeletal malignancy overall?
back: Metastatic tumors (most common from prostate, breast, kidney, and lung cancers).
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1197 (Book Page): [Metastatic tumors are the most common form of skeletal malignancy, greatly outnumbering primary bone cancers.]

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and radiological findings of bone, cartilaginous and soft tumors
front: Q: What are the classic clinical and radiological hallmarks of an Osteoid Osteoma?
back: - Clinical: Severe nocturnal pain relieved by aspirin or NSAIDs. - Radiology: A radiolucent nidus (less than 2cm) surrounded by a thick rim of reactive cortical bone. - Predilection: Appendicular skeleton (femur/tibia) in young men.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1189 (Book Page): [osteoid osteomas present with severe nocturnal pain that is probably caused by prostaglandin E2 (PGE2) produced by the proliferating osteoblasts and is relieved by aspirin... nidus, which forms a small radiolucent core... surrounded by abundant reactive bone.]

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and radiological findings of bone, cartilaginous and soft tumors
front: Q: Discuss the molecular etiology and genetic mutations typically identified in primary Osteosarcoma.
back: - RB mutations: Found in 70% of sporadic cases; germline mutations increase risk 1000-fold. - TP53 mutations: Associated with Li-Fraumeni syndrome. - CDKN2A inactivation: Affects p16 and p14. - MDM2/CDK4: Overexpressed via 12q13-q15 amplification in low-grade variants.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1189 (Book Page): [Approximately 70% of osteosarcomas have acquired genetic abnormalities... RB mutations are present in up to 70% of sporadic osteosarcomas; germline RB mutations confer a 1000-fold increased risk... TP53 is mutated in the germline of individuals with Li-Fraumeni syndrome.]

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and radiological findings of bone, cartilaginous and soft tumors
front: Q: Differentiate the characteristic periosteal reactions of Ewing Sarcoma from Osteosarcoma on X-ray.
back: - Ewing Sarcoma: 'Onion-skin' appearance (concentric layers of reactive bone). - Osteosarcoma: Codman Triangle (triangular shadow between the cortex and raised periosteal ends). - Significance: Both indicate aggressive tumor growth lifting the periosteum from the bone.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1189 (Book Page) & 1193: [The triangular shadow between the cortex and raised periosteal ends, known radiographically as a Codman triangle... characteristic periosteal reaction produces layers of reactive bone deposited in an onion-skin fashion.]

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and radiological findings of bone, cartilaginous and soft tumors
front: Q: A 15-year-old male presents with knee pain and a blastic mass showing a 'Codman Triangle'. Diagnosis?
back: - Diagnosis: Osteosarcoma. - Morphology: Malignant mesenchymal tumor cells directly producing unmineralized osteoid or mineralized woven bone. - Clinical: Most common primary malignant bone tumor; 75% occur before age 20, usually near the knee.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1189 (Book Page): [Osteosarcoma is the most common primary malignant tumor of bone... Codman triangle, indicates an aggressive tumor... Diagnosis of osteosarcoma requires the presence of malignant tumor cells producing unmineralized osteoid or mineralized bone.]

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and radiological findings of bone, cartilaginous and soft tumors
front: Q: Explain the pathophysiology of localized bone resorption in Giant Cell Tumor (Osteoclastoma).
back: - Neoplastic primitive osteoblast precursors overexpress RANKL. - RANKL drives proliferation and differentiation of non-neoplastic osteoclast precursors into mature, destructive osteoclasts. - Location: Usually epiphysis of long bones (distal femur/proximal tibia) in adults aged 20-40.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1194 (Book Page): [neoplastic cells are primitive osteoblast precursors that express high levels of RANKL, which in turn promotes the proliferation of osteoclast precursors and their differentiation into mature osteoclasts... localized, but highly destructive, bone resorption.]

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and radiological findings of bone, cartilaginous and soft tumors
front: Q: What are the defining morphological and radiological findings of conventional Chondrosarcoma?
back: - Morphology: Large bulky nodules of glistening gray-white or myxoid cartilage infiltrating marrow spaces. - Radiology: Flocculent densities (calcified matrix) with cortical destruction and soft tissue mass formation. - Demographics: Typically affects adults aged 40+ in the axial skeleton.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1193 (Book Page): [Conventional chondrosarcomas are large bulky tumors made up of nodules of glistening gray-white, translucent cartilage... Neoplastic cartilage infiltrates the marrow space and surrounds preexisting bony trabeculae... calcified matrix of chondrosarcomas appears as foci of flocculent densities.]

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and radiological findings of bone, cartilaginous and soft tumors
front: Q: Describe the genetic etiology and pathogenesis of Multiple Hereditary Exostosis Syndrome.
back: - Etiology: Germline loss-of-function mutations in EXT1 or EXT2. - Pathogenesis: Defective synthesis of heparan sulfate glycosaminoglycans disrupts Indian hedgehog (Ihh) signaling. - Result: Disorganized growth plate cartilage forms a bony stalk with a cartilage cap (Osteochondroma).
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1191 (Book Page): [Hereditary exostoses are associated with germline loss-of-function mutations in either the EXT1 or the EXT2 gene... Reduced or abnormal glycosaminoglycans may prevent normal diffusion of Indian hedgehog (Ihh)... thereby disrupting Hedgehog signaling and chondrocyte differentiation.]

category: Discuss the etiology, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical manifestations and radiological findings of bone, cartilaginous and soft tumors
front: Q: A girl presents with polyostotic bone lesions, café-au-lait spots, and precocious puberty. Identify the syndrome and mutation.
back: - Syndrome: McCune-Albright Syndrome. - Genetic Defect: Somatic gain-of-function mutations in GNAS1 (constitutively active Gs-alpha). - Pathology: Fibrous dysplasia; curvilinear trabeculae of woven bone (C-shaped/Chinese figures) without prominent osteoblastic rimming in a fibrous background.
citation: In book "Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine", Page 1196 (Book Page): [McCune-Albright syndrome: polyostotic disease, associated with café-au-lait skin pigmentations and endocrine abnormalities... somatic gain-of-function mutations in GNAS1... curvilinear trabeculae of woven bone surrounded by... fibroblastic proliferation without prominent osteoblastic rimming.]
